chunks.about-about#0:
Software engineer working on AI agents, retrieval systems and reproducible evaluation. Currently pursuing an M.Tech. in Software Engineering at the National University of Singapore. I build systems that turn model outputs into controlled, executable actions, then measure how well they work.

I studied Computer Science at KAIST before joining NUS. My experience spans enterprise agents, industrial computer vision and Java Web development.

My independent projects explore coding agents built from first principles, multi-path retrieval and context management. Controlled experiments, including negative results, guide the design.
chunks.about-about#1: From Java Web development to industrial vision and enterprise agents, my focus has remained on execution boundaries, real-world performance and reproducible evidence.

Worked to cost-reduction briefs from engineering, product planning and project management in Shanghai from February to July 2026, and led a ~20-person data group from April.

Team lead: led the AI enablement team’s data group of about 20 from April 2026 — daily stand-ups, an owner and a product manager paired to every business request, delivery tracked through acceptance, and the team’s shared LLM budget and API keys.
chunks.about-experience#1:
Connector selection agent: in production with the vehicle-architecture team. The company’s rollout poster credits it with cutting a selection from 10–15 minutes of manual lookup, or up to 48 hours waiting on suppliers, to 2–3 minutes, across five product collections and 143 part specifications. I took over a 1.6k-line prototype and owned development through four iterations, growing it into an 8.5k-line Flask, LangChain and MongoDB system.

The decision worth describing: removing the LLM call that wrote the database query. The model only parses one sentence into exact, fuzzy and range filters on a fixed JSON schema, and the query is built by deterministic code — so a wrong answer localises immediately to either parsing or rules.
chunks.about-experience#2:
PRD review agent: multimodal input (one-liners, links, audio and video, drafts) with completeness diagnosis, Mermaid flowcharts and write-back to Feishu docs. In use on Dify, with a LangChain port beginning at handover.

Retrieval and reuse: built the five-path retrieval of BodyCraft, an engineering-document search system used by about 100 body engineers, and co-built the team’s skill-asset platform with two colleagues, designing its unified MCP calling interface.

Also contributed to the team’s conversational spreadsheet-analysis platform (see Projects), owning its backend storage and async layer and joining the patent filing as one of the inventors.
chunks.about-experience#3:

Worked on an examination system with the municipal emergency-management bureau. Four to five synchronized cameras assess procedural compliance and completeness. The system ran live exams every working day for over a month; I owned three examination scenarios across two trades and set the annotation specification with the data department.
chunks.about-experience#4:
Replaced YOLO detection plus hand-written rules with graph-based scoring. YOLOv8 extracts component centres, sizes, angles and classes; assembly constraints connect them into a graph, and a graph convolutional network predicts installation and step-completion states.

Models reached around 90% accuracy in internal acceptance testing. Human co-invigilation and tablet scoring provided a fallback so an algorithm failure would not interrupt an exam.

chunks.about-projects#0:
A decision-support agent that turns supplier quotes into comparable evidence. Code produces a reference ranking, the agent makes a recommendation using read-only tools, and a buyer approves or overrides it.

A four-person team project for the NUS-ISS “Show Me Your Agent” hackathon, demonstrated with synthetic supplier data.

Normalizes price, lead time, payment terms, on-time delivery and quality; applies hard constraints before calculating reference scores and negotiation gaps.

Calls a model through an Ollama-compatible gateway and parses JSON tool requests. The agent may depart from the reference ranking when supported by tool evidence; structured output is validated.
chunks.about-projects#1:

Logs model recommendations, buyer approvals or override reasons, and request IDs. The system recommends; it never places orders.

chunks.about-projects#5:
A command-line coding assistant built without an agent framework. Repository maps, sandbox escape tests and A/A controls put each design decision to the test.

A native tool-calling ReAct loop with seven tools. SEARCH/REPLACE editing uses a four-tier matching chain to handle whitespace and partial-line drift. Shell commands run inside macOS Seatbelt, with boundaries verified by escape tests. About 1,140 lines of core code under 60 tests, 12 of them on sandbox policy.
chunks.about-projects#6:
The repository map uses tree-sitter definitions and references to build a file graph, then personalized PageRank to rank context for the task. Constraining edges by actual Python imports raised edge precision from 32% to 100% without dropping a true edge. IDF-weighted seeds addressed query understanding.

On a 112-file repository, the map reduced task steps by 21% and input tokens by 33%. Read that next to its noise: an A/A arm put the input-token noise floor at about 26%, so the 33% sits only just above it, and at n=1 the figure was +6%. It describes that controlled experiment, not a guarantee.
chunks.about-projects#7:
The evaluation harness runs an A/A arm by default, putting effects beside their noise floor; this led me to retract an earlier claim. In this architecture, output caps made history compression unnecessary. Sub-agent isolation used 71% more total tokens (184,130 delegated against 107,466 not delegated, a 1.71x ratio) for 22% less main-loop context, with no gain in completion or correctness. Raw traces are committed.

chunks.about-projects#8:
An agent that does mathematics research on its own: a lead splits the work among readers, real computation runs in a sandbox, and every step and its cost streams live and can be steered. I owned the layer that makes that spending accountable.

The project (team-built): readers search arXiv, OpenAlex and the OEIS in parallel and run real computation in a network-less Docker sandbox with Python (NumPy, SymPy, NetworkX, Matplotlib). Every step and its cost streams to the browser live, and you can message a running task, stop it, or edit your last message and run it again.
chunks.about-projects#9:
I owned the server-side billing module: a wallet ledger with atomic per-task expenses, an ordered budget responsibility chain, a default per-account cap with an approval flow, Stripe test-mode top-ups with receipts, authenticated encryption for user-supplied API keys, and staff account administration with actor checks.

Why that layer matters: this agent calls models and runs computation on its own, which means it spends money on its own. A budget has to be able to refuse an action before it runs, refusals have to leave a trail, approvals have to be attributable, and ledger ownership has to survive account deletion.
chunks.about-projects#10:
Every feature commit ships with its own test file — ledger, budget chain, Stripe, key encryption, approval lifecycle and HTTP boundaries. Keeping that discipline inside a codebase someone else leads is what I took away from this project.

Attribution: the project is led by ziyangliu-666 (170 commits); I am the second contributor with 32 of about 227. Parallel scheduling, literature search and sandboxed execution were other members’ work.

chunks.about-projects#11:
Freeze a scoped quantitative research experiment, audit its replay accounting, and export independently verifiable evidence.

A research claim, its data binding and its execution assumptions are frozen before any replay is allowed, and the resulting evidence bundle can be re-audited offline without installing the replay engine.

The coordinator holds sole research-write authority: original budgets, retries and acknowledgements each leave a trail, and committed outcomes can be reverified without re-execution.

The current trust boundary is M0, a trusted single owner; registered Python source is not executed. M1 restricted isolation is unimplemented, and process supervision and hashes do not constitute a malicious-code sandbox.

An open-source re-implementation of the five-path retrieval I built at SAIC, with per-path score breakdowns and weights treated as a measurable ranking problem rather than a matter of taste. Design complete, implementation in progress.

Runs filename and path, section title, SQLite FTS5, dense-vector and entity-graph retrieval in parallel. Results merge per file with per-path scores exposed.

Index schemas, configuration and ranking metrics (NDCG, MRR, Hit@K) are covered by 17 tests. The pipeline runs offline without an API key.

chunks.about-research#0:
Rong He | 2026-10-10 | Preprint · arXiv v1

Tests whether failure feedback steers an agent’s self-modification toward a specific failure. Across 145 eligible edits in public Darwin Gödel Machine logs, no target-specific advantage was detected. Controlled instruction-revision studies found model-dependent benefits from relevant feedback, while target repair did not reliably improve held-out performance. The work separates target repair, transfer to related failures and held-out net change.

arXiv: [arXiv:2610.14662](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14662)
chunks.about-research#1:
Rong He | 2026-10-01 | Preprint · Zenodo v1

How should a best-of-n deployment budget be chosen from a fixed candidate pool with limited correctness labels? This work gives matching minimax expected-regret bounds for adaptive and non-adaptive labelling. The extra logarithmic cost of non-adaptivity affects only the label term. The bounds account for pool size, label budget and menu width. Exact checks and synthetic diagnostics illustrate finite-budget limits; they do not establish gains on real tasks.

Zenodo: [10.5281/zenodo.23086434](https://zenodo.org/records/23086434)
chunks.about-research#2:
Rong He | 2026-09-28 | Preprint · Zenodo v1.0

Compares a finite menu of Boolean queries that return either a truth value at an unknown state or an exact population probability. For pointwise minimax error e and population minimax excess zero-one risk R, proves e ≤ R ≤ 2e. Equality is universally preserved when e = 0 or e ≥ 1/3; every attainable error between 0 and 1/3 admits an interface with R > e. The result concerns exact, restricted query interfaces, not model performance.

Zenodo: [10.5281/zenodo.23020314](https://zenodo.org/records/23020314)
chunks.about-research#3:
Rong He | 2026-09-15 | Preprint · arXiv v1

Studies what task decomposition buys and loses: smaller root context, but less of the information discovered by leaves surviving the journey back. Models retention as r(b) = 1/b, validates it on 20,000 irregular trees, and analyses 600 production deep-research traces and 743,819 tool calls. Flat structures are optimal for yield; decomposition earns its keep through context integrity and cost.

arXiv: [arXiv:2609.17464](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.17464)
chunks.about-research#4:
Rong He | 2026-09-12 | Preprint · arXiv v1

Recasts the ordering of reusable prompt chunks as a binary-hierarchy problem over requests, identifying when a fixed global order is suboptimal. On BM25 retrieval traces from three BEIR corpora, the layout reduces prefill computation by 17–36% compared with production RAG ordering.

arXiv: [arXiv:2609.13692](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.13692)
chunks.about-research#5:
Rong He | 2026-09-10 | Preprint · Zenodo v0.10

Constructs stationary binary hidden Markov models with strictly positive transitions and emissions whose observations conceal the direction of time at any 2n − 4 sampling instants. Establishes a matching, sharp sample-complexity bound for detection.
